facts.statement: Fossils of Juncitarsus were collected in 1946 and 1947 in the Bridger Formation of Wyoming by Charles Lewis Gazin, Franklin L. Pearce, and George F. Sternberg.
facts.quote: A small set of bones were collected in 1946 and 1947 by Charles Lewis Gazin, Franklin L. Pearce, and George F. Sternberg at a locality in the Bridger Formation of Wyoming.

facts.statement: The genus Juncitarsus was formally named in 1980 by Storrs L. Olson and Alan Feduccia.
facts.quote: It was not until 1980 that they were named by Storrs L. Olson and Alan Feduccia.

facts.statement: A second species, J. merkeli, was named in 1987 by Stefan Peters based on fossils from Germany.
facts.quote: A second species, J. merkeli from Germany was named in 1987 by Stefan Peters.

facts.statement: Juncitarsus lived during the Eocene epoch in the United States and Germany.
facts.quote: Juncitarsus is an extinct genus of wading birds from the Eocene of the United States and Germany.

facts.statement: Fossil remains of J. gracillimus include at least three adults or near-adults and one chick that could not fly when it died.
facts.quote: The remains of J. gracillimus belong to at least three adult or nearly adult birds and one chick, which at the time of death could not fly.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests that Juncitarsus lived in colonies as a wading bird.
facts.quote: Based on the available evidence, Juncitarsus was a colonial species of wading bird.

facts.statement: Juncitarsus is likely a basal member of the Mirandornithes clade and is not a true flamingo.
facts.quote: Though previously considered a flamingo, it is likely outside of Phoenicopteridae, possibly a basal member of the Mirandornithes (neither Phoenicopteriformes or Podicipediformes).

facts.statement: Current classification considers Juncitarsus a basal member of the Mirandornithes.
facts.quote: In light of this, Juncitarsus has been considered to be a basal mirandornithean.

facts.statement: Juncitarsus fossils are found in the Bridger Formation of Wyoming and the Messel Pit of Germany, dating from the Ypresian to Lutetian stages of the Eocene.
facts.quote: Juncitarsus is known from both the Bridger Formation of Wyoming and the Messel Pit of Germany dating from the Ypresian to the Lutetian stages of the Eocene epoch.

facts.statement: Juncitarsus lived between 51.1 and 37.71 million years ago during the Ypresian to Bartonian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Ypresian to Bartonian (51.1 to 37.71 million years ago)

facts.statement: Researchers originally debated whether Juncitarsus was the earliest flamingo or related to avocets and stilts due to similarities with Recurvirostridae.
facts.quote: Olson and Feduccia had originally classified Juncitarsus as the earliest known member of the flamingo family Phoenicopteridae, though due its overall similarity to the family Recurvirostridae that authors suggested a kinship between flamingos and the avocets and stilts.

facts.statement: The wading lifestyle of Juncitarsus is considered a derived feature that evolved independently from its swimming waterbird ancestors.
facts.quote: Despite this wading lifestyle, this is actually a derived featured for this genus in respect to later mirandornitheans as it is believed this was required independently between Phoenicopteriformes and Juncitarsus.

rejected.quote: The nominate species was named J. gracillimus with the nomenclature meaning 'slender reed ankle'.
